lead: A VLSI design flow is the ordered set of stages that turns a written specification into a tested silicon chip. A chip with millions of gates cannot be designed in one jump, so each stage solves a smaller, checkable problem. Front-end work (specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis) and back-end work (DFT insertion, floorplan, placement, clock tree, routing, signoff) end at tapeout, when the final layout goes to the foundry; fabrication, wafer test, packaging and final test follow. Phone SoCs, set-top box chips and payment-terminal chips are all made this way.
prereq: You need: basic digital logic (gates, flip-flops, Boolean algebra, binary numbers); the rest of this chapter starts from zero.

blocks.text: Each stage takes one description of the chip, produces a more concrete one and hands a checked file to the next.

items: Specification: function, clock frequency in MHz or GHz, power in W, cost, package, interfaces.
Architecture: partition into blocks, count clock domains, fix bus widths, memory sizes and I/O pins.
RTL: write the design as register-transfer-level Verilog modules (Verilog HDL, modelling styles).
Verification: simulate against a test bench (test benches) and add formal proofs.
Synthesis: map RTL to a gate netlist of standard cells under a clock-period constraint.
DFT insertion: add scan chains and self-test logic while the design is still a netlist.
Physical design: floorplan, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing (floorplanning, placement and routing).
Signoff: design-rule check (DRC), layout versus schematic (LVS), static timing, power and IR drop.
Tapeout: the final layout database (GDSII or OASIS) is handed to the foundry for mask making. Tapeout is only this handoff.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this the ASIC design flow. The order is top-down (specification to blocks, blocks to RTL, RTL to gates), but real projects also reuse verified blocks bottom-up. Verification is not one box: RTL simulation starts it; after synthesis, equivalence checking proves the netlist does what the RTL does; after routing, static timing analysis and gate-level simulation check the real wires.

After tapeout the foundry makes one photomask per layer and builds hundreds of identical dies on a silicon wafer, today usually 300 mm across. The process steps themselves are covered under CMOS fabrication and layout; the chip goes through them in this order.

items: Front-end-of-line: wells, isolation, gate oxide, gates and source-drain implants build the transistors.
Back-end-of-line: contacts, then layers of metal wires and vias in insulating oxide, connect them.
Wafer probe (wafer sort): a probe card touches each die's pads for a short test; failing dies are marked on a wafer map.
Dicing and packaging: the wafer is sawn into dies; good dies are bonded and sealed in packages.
Final test: each packaged chip is tested again on automatic test equipment (ATE), then binned and shipped.

blocks.text: Yield = good dies ÷ total dies. It is never 100 %, and a bad chip found in a customer's phone costs far more than one found on the tester.

sections.h3: Block-level choices and SoC verification issues

blocks.text: At block level the flow fixes the details that sink projects late: the clock plan (PLL, clock domains, resets), the I/O ring (pads, electrostatic discharge protection), the device modes (functional, scan, self-test, sleep), the memories (compiled SRAM macros), the analog blocks (PLL, ADC, regulator) and power management (power gating, isolation cells, retention flip-flops). A wrong clock decision found at signoff costs weeks; found in the specification it costs an hour. Which style builds the gates is the subject of the next chapter.

A complex chip or SoC is hard to verify and test because: (1) its state space is too large to simulate fully, so teams measure coverage and add formal proofs and emulation; (2) embedded IP cores sit deep inside, so their pins are not chip pins and tests must reach them through a wrapper (IP cores); (3) several clock and power domains add crossing and power-up bugs; (4) analog blocks need their own tests; (5) firmware must be verified with the hardware.

The design team hands the test team three things: the DUT (device under test, as a netlist), the inserted DFT hardware, and the pattern set. ATPG (automatic test pattern generation) makes the patterns from the netlist and a fault model; fault simulation grades them as fault coverage in percent. BIST (built-in self-test) puts a pattern generator and checker on the chip itself, commonly for memories.

head: Fault model
What it models
rows: A line too slow to rise or fall
A short that shows only while switching
A tiny extra delay below TDF resolution

blocks.text: In scan design each flip-flop gets a multiplexer, and in test mode the flip-flops join into a shift register (a scan chain): a pattern is shifted in, captured in one clock and shifted out. Boundary scan (IEEE 1149.1, JTAG) puts a scan cell at every I/O pin behind the test access port TDI, TDO, TCK and TMS (TRST optional). Turning patterns into a tester program with timing, levels and compare strobes is the test-coding step; STIL (IEEE 1450) is a common format for it.
test time = (N × (L + 1) + L) × T<sub>clk</sub>,   cost = test time × tester rate
blocks.where: N is the number of patterns, L the longest chain in flip-flops, T<sub>clk</sub> the scan clock period and the tester rate in rupees per second. Shifting in the next pattern overlaps shifting out the last, so each pattern costs L + 1 cycles, plus one final unload of L. Fault models, ATPG, scan and BIST are taught in full under VLSI testing and design for testability.

examples.question: An SoC has 24 lakh standard-cell gates. Synthesis runs at 1,20,000 gates per hour, placement and routing together run at 60,000 gates per hour, and verification needs 3 hours per 10,000 gates. Find the synthesis time, the physical-design time, the verification time, the total flow time, and the verification share of that total.
steps: Total time = 20 h + 40 h + 720 h = 780 h.
examples.answer: Synthesis 20 h, physical design 40 h, verification 720 h, total 780 h; verification is 92.3 % of the flow.

examples.question: A chip has 5,000 scan flip-flops. ATPG gives 1,000 patterns, the scan clock is 50 MHz and the test house charges ₹3 per second of tester time. Find the test time and test cost per chip (a) with one scan chain of 5,000 flip-flops and (b) with ten chains of 500. (c) What does the change save on 10 lakh chips?
steps: Scan clock period: T<sub>clk</sub> = 1 ÷ 50 MHz = 20 ns.
(b) Ten chains shift in parallel, so L = 500: cycles = 1,000 × 501 + 500 = 5,01,500; time = 10.03 ms; cost = 0.01003 s × ₹3/s = ₹0.0301.
(c) On 10 lakh chips: (a) costs ₹3,00,360 and (b) costs ₹30,090, so ten chains save ₹2,70,270 of tester time.
Check: L falls 10 times and the time falls from 100.12 ms to 10.03 ms, almost 10 times (the capture cycles do not shrink).
examples.answer: One chain: 100.12 ms, ₹0.300 per chip. Ten chains: 10.03 ms, ₹0.0301 per chip, saving about ₹2.7 lakh on 10 lakh chips at the cost of 20 scan pins.

traps: Do not draw the flow as one line with test at the end: verification runs beside it from RTL to signoff, and DFT insertion comes before physical design.
The front end ends at the gate netlist (synthesis), not at RTL.
Tapeout is only the handoff of the final layout for mask making; fabrication, probe, packaging and final test come after it.
DFT is not testing: DFT adds hardware during design; the tester applies ATPG patterns after fabrication.
High stuck-at coverage does not mean zero escapes: delay defects, bridging and Iddq need their own models.

quiz.q: Define the front-end and back-end parts of the VLSI design flow.
quiz.a: Front-end: specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, ending at the gate netlist. Back-end: DFT insertion, floorplan, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing, signoff and tapeout.

quiz.q: What does ATPG produce, and what does fault simulation do with it?
quiz.a: ATPG produces test patterns from the netlist and a fault model; fault simulation reports the fraction of modelled faults those patterns detect, as coverage in percent.

quiz.q: Name the four compulsory pins of the boundary-scan test access port.
quiz.a: TDI (test data in), TDO (test data out), TCK (test clock) and TMS (test mode select); TRST is optional.

quiz.q: Give one reason DFT insertion is placed before physical design.
quiz.a: The added scan chains and self-test logic must be placed, buffered and timed with the rest of the logic. Inserting them after routing would change the netlist and break timing and design rules.

quiz.q: A chip has 2,000 scan flip-flops in 4 equal chains, 800 patterns and a 25 MHz scan clock. Find the scan test time.
A team tapes out at 99.8% stuck-at coverage. One chip fails at full clock speed in the lab. Which fault models were probably not covered, and why?
quiz.a: Stuck-at patterns catch lines fixed at 0 or 1, usually applied slowly. A part that works slowly but fails at speed points to transition delay, path delay or small delay defects, and possibly resistive bridging; these need at-speed transition and path patterns.

beyond: Not for the exam. Open-source flows built from Yosys (synthesis) and OpenROAD (placement and routing) with public process design kits let students tape out small chips. Chiplets and 2.5D packaging split one big die into several verified dies joined by short links, which moves test to the package boundary. Search next: SDC timing constraints, UPF power intent and chiplet test.
